name: Absent-Mindedness
description: Absent-mindedness is a family of everyday memory failures caused by lapses of attention: the mind is elsewhere when information or an intended action should be encoded or retrieved. It often shows up as misplacing things, forgetting routine intentions, or losing track of what one was doing mid-task.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to interruptions, backgrounded tasks, reminders, autosave, checklists, and return-to-task flows. It matters most where products rely on users remembering routine intentions under distraction, but it is not a mainstream named interface law in ordinary design critique.
myth_risk_note: The label 'absent-mindedness' conflates multiple distinct phenomena (attention lapses, transient forgetting, blocking) under one colloquial umbrella. Schacter, Chiao & Mitchell's (2003) framework and the surrounding empirical work show these operate via different mechanisms, meaning the single-construct framing risks oversimplifying a genuinely heterogeneous family of attention/memory failures.
prevalence_note: A familiar everyday and psychology term that occasionally matters in reminder/checklist/task-resumption design, but rarely cited as a named canonical UX law.

findings.description: Developed and validated the Cognitive Failures Questionnaire (CFQ), a self-report measure of everyday absent-mindedness-type slips in perception, memory, and motor function. The measure correlates with independent spouse ratings (real external validity, not just self-perception), is stable over time like a trait rather than a transient state, and predicts vulnerability to stress effects in psychiatric symptoms specifically among people in stressful jobs -- suggesting absent-mindedness is a real, measurable individual-difference vulnerability factor rather than a purely situational effect. The foundational, most-cited paper (2,961 citations) establishing everyday cognitive-failure measurement as a real, valid construct.
findings.source_title: The Cognitive Failures Questionnaire (CFQ) and its correlates

findings.description: Schacter's review characterizes absent-mindedness as memory failure caused by breakdowns at the interface between attention and memory, where distraction or divided attention disrupts the encoding or later retrieval of everyday information and intended actions.
findings.source_title: The seven sins of memory: Insights from psychology and cognitive neuroscience.
